title: How Paul wrote
hook: letters dictated to real churches with real problems, before the gospels were written

segments.voice: Yesterday, Rome, and Acts ending on the word unhindered. Your line was without hindrance. Who came through your door? Day five hundred fifty-nine.

A box of old family letters, found in an attic. Not speeches. Letters. Answers to questions nobody wrote down, jokes that need context, names no one remembers, a worry about money, a fight between cousins, and then, in the middle of it all, a paragraph worth reading twice. That's the kind of thing we're opening today. A new part of the path: the letters of the New Testament, and first, the letters of Paul.
screen: `A BOX OF OLD LETTERS.` → `QUESTIONS WE CAN'T SEE.` → `A NEW PART: THE LETTERS.`

segments.voice: The word is epistle, from the Greek epistole, simply a letter, something sent. And here's the first surprise: a common scholarly view places Paul's letters before the Gospels were written down. On that view, opening Paul means hearing a voice from the first Christian generation, writing to churches that were still new. Second, Paul didn't always hold the pen. At times he dictated to a secretary. At the end of Romans, the secretary even slips in his own greeting. In the Douay-Rheims: "I Tertius, who wrote this epistle, salute you in the Lord." Then, in several letters, Paul takes the pen for the last lines, as a signature. To the Galatians he writes: "See what a letter I have written to you with my own hand." The Greek speaks of large letters: big handwriting, his own. Third, these were real letters to real people with real problems. Corinth is split into factions. The Galatians are confused. The Thessalonians are grieving their dead. Paul answers them, scolds them, misses them, and greets friends by name. The letters were carried by hand and read aloud to the whole church. A whole set of New Testament letters carries Paul's name. Scholars debate whether he wrote every one himself or whether some come from his close followers; the Church receives all of them as scripture. At Sunday Mass, the second reading often comes from these letters. You're hearing someone else's mail, and it was meant to be shared.
screen: `EPISTOLE: A LETTER, SOMETHING SENT.` · `LIKELY BEFORE THE GOSPELS.` · `DICTATED, THEN SIGNED IN BIG LETTERS.` · `REAL CHURCHES, REAL PROBLEMS.` · then, large: `READ ALOUD TO EVERYONE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: write a short letter to someone. Settle, and breathe. Think of a person you haven't really written to in a long time. Not a text. A letter, even a short one. What would you say to them, if it were the kind of thing that might be kept? Thanks for something specific. A memory. Encouragement for something hard they're facing. Compose three sentences in your head now. Maybe later, write them down, and sign them in your own big letters. If you pray, you can pray for that person as Paul so often did in his opening lines. The bell holds the time.
Epistle. A letter, something sent: Paul's dictated, hand-signed letters to real churches, read aloud to everyone. Today's word.
Your line: real letters to real people. Today, write a few honest lines to someone, by hand if you can. Day five hundred fifty-nine.

howItsDone: At Sunday Mass, Catholics usually hear three readings, and the second is most often from the New Testament letters, many of them Paul's; it is read aloud to the whole assembly, as the letters first were.
